newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU revamps food safety services after BSE scare.
newsitem.headline: EU revamps food safety services after BSE scare.

text.p: A major reorganisation of the European Commission's food safety services was announced on Wednesday as the EU's executive fought to avoid possible censure from the European Parliament for mishandling the mad cow crisis.
The Parliament on February 19 will debate a report by a special committee of inquiry which attacks the Commission and Britain for making serious errors.
A censure motion may be presented, which if it gains the required two-thirds majority of votes cast, would force the Commission President Jacques Santer and his 19 colleagues to resign.

"The Commission, in order to provide the necessary political impulse and to coordinate its actions, has created a group of commissioners to oversee food health," the EU's executive said in a statement.
The group, which will be chaired by Santer, would include the the EU commissioners for consumer affairs, agriculture, industry, public health and possibly research.
Consumer affairs commissioner Emma Bonino, will play a key role, having been given responsibility for consumer health. Her fledgling directorate will be considerably reinforced.

The dynamic and tireless Italian commissioner was recently made "European of the Year" for her efforts to give the EU a Seven scientific, veterinary and food committees advising on BSE measures will report directly to her.

"The confusion of responsibilities could give rise to criticism," commission chief spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas told a news briefing, adding the commission will present within two months proposals to make the committees more efficient.

The shake-up is a blow for the EU executive's powerful agriculture directorate, which previously drafted and implemented measures to combat the disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), and checked how well they were enforced.
It has been criticised for giving priority to aiding beef farmers rather than protecting public health.

In another move, the Commission also gave control of a new veterinary inspection office -- which will be based in Ireland -- to Bonino. The office could eventually develop into an independent food safety agency.
A special unit to evaluate public health risks will also be put under Bonino's control.

But the changes, promised last month by Santer, are unlikely to appease the European Parliament, which is frustrated at its lack of power to take action against Britain, which it holds mainly responsible for mismanaging the mad cow crisis.
It wants the commission to take Britain to the European Court of Justice to seek damages for losses causes by the crisis and senior EU Commission officials to be sanctioned.
